notes.b: Geographers divide the earth into regions so that places can be studied as groups instead of one by one. A region is an area of the earth's surface that shares one or more characteristics, called criteria, which make it different from the areas around it.
points: Physical criteria: climate (the usual weather of a place), relief (the height and shape of the land) and rock type, such as limestone.
Administrative criteria: the boundaries set by government, such as county lines.
Cultural criteria: language and religion, which separate groups of people.
Socio-economic criteria: wealth, employment and development (how advanced a place's economy and living standards are).
Urban criteria: a city and its hinterland (the surrounding area that depends on the city for services and jobs).
These five types of region are the five subsections of this chapter, and this subsection deals with physical regions.
notes.tip: Short questions ask you to match types of region to definitions or examples, so learn the five criteria and what each one means.

notes.h: Scale, indices and boundaries of regions
notes.b: Regions can be big or small, and they can be defined by one criterion or by several. Their edges also differ: some are fixed by law, others fade gradually.
points: Regions exist at different scales. A local region is a county or a city's hinterland, e.g. Co. Clare; a national region is the West of Ireland; a continental region is North West Europe; a global region is the Islamic world.
A single index (one measurable criterion) defines a region by that one thing: rock type alone gives a karst region (a limestone landscape shaped by water dissolving the rock).

Multiple indices combine several criteria. For example, a peripheral region (one on the edge of a country's economic activity, far from its centre) can be defined by income, unemployment and out-migration (people leaving the area) together.
Physical and cultural regions usually merge into their neighbours through transition zones (a gradual belt of change) rather than ending at a sharp line.
Administrative regions have exact boundaries, fixed by law, so you can say precisely which side of the line a place lies on.
Regions also change over time as their criteria change.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain and illustrate the idea of a region at different scales, so give one named example for each scale: Co. Clare, the West of Ireland, North West Europe and the Islamic world.

notes.b: Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years. A climatic region is a large area with similar temperature, precipitation (rain, snow and other moisture falling from the sky) and seasonal pattern, usually with similar natural vegetation and soils.
points: The world can be divided into climatic regions. This subsection studies the cool temperate oceanic type in detail.
Cool temperate oceanic: Ireland and North West Europe, which is why Ireland is the case studied here.
Warm temperate oceanic: the Mediterranean type, with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, so it differs from Ireland.
Hot desert: e.g. the Sahara.
notes.tip: Warm temperate oceanic is the Mediterranean climate, not Ireland's. Ireland is cool temperate oceanic, and exams use warm temperate oceanic and hot desert as distractors. In matching questions the climatic regions are cool temperate oceanic, warm temperate oceanic, the Mediterranean and hot desert.

notes.h: Characteristics of the cool temperate oceanic climate
notes.b: The cool temperate oceanic climate is mild and wet, with no extremes of heat or cold. These are the features to describe, with the Irish figures (Met Éireann long-term averages).
points: Mild winters, because of the warm sea: mean January (coldest month) temperatures are about 4-7°C.
Cool summers, so it is never hot: mean July (warmest month) temperatures are about 14-16°C.
The annual range of temperature (the gap between the warmest and coldest month) is small, only about 10°C, and snow is rare on low ground.
Rain falls in every month, so there is no dry season.
The weather is changeable, with prevailing (most frequent) south-westerly winds.
notes.tip: A 30-mark Higher question on how climate can define regions expects the cool temperate oceanic characteristics with Irish figures, so learn the temperature and rainfall figures given here. Use only these figures, not ones from past-paper answers.

notes.b: Ireland's climate comes from several causes working together: where it sits on the globe, the ocean beside it and the winds that cross it. Each cause explains one feature of the climate.
points: Latitude: Ireland lies between about 51.5°N and 55.5°N, in the mid-latitudes, where the sun's angle is moderate, so it is neither very hot nor very cold.
North Atlantic Drift: a warm ocean current, the extension of the Gulf Stream, keeps winters mild and coasts free of ice.
Maritime influence (the effect of being close to the sea): the sea heats and cools slowly, so the annual temperature range is small.
Prevailing south-westerly winds blow off the Atlantic, carrying its mild, moist air over Ireland.

Frequent Atlantic depressions (areas of low pressure that bring wind and rain) and their fronts (the boundaries between warm and cold air) bring rain. These weather systems are taught in the Weather and Climate chapter.
Relief rainfall: moist air is forced up the western mountains, cools and releases its rain on their western slopes.
notes.tip: The controls of the climate are part of the expected answer to the 30-mark question on how climate can define regions. Give each control with its effect, for example the North Atlantic Drift with mild winters.

notes.b: The climate is not the same everywhere in Ireland. Because the wet south-westerly winds arrive from the Atlantic, the west gets the most rain and the east the least.
points: The west is wetter than the east: about 1,000-1,250 mm of rain a year across much of the west, against about 750 mm in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin.
Over 2,000 mm a year falls on many western mountains, because moist air is forced to rise over them.
The east lies in a rain shadow (a drier area on the sheltered side of high ground), protected from the south-westerly winds by the western uplands.
Wet days (days with measurable rain): about 150 a year on the east and south-east coasts, rising to about 225 a year in parts of the west.
The south-east is the sunniest region, because it is sheltered from the wet south-westerlies.
The north is slightly cooler than the south, and coasts are milder in winter than the inland Midlands, because the sea warms them.
notes.tip: The 30-mark question on climate regions expects variation within Ireland, so give west against east with the rainfall figures.

notes.h: North West Europe and the eastward transition
notes.b: North West Europe is the international setting for this climate, because the same conditions that affect Ireland affect its neighbours. Further east the climate changes step by step.
points: The same climate covers Ireland, Britain, north-west France (Brittany), Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and coastal Norway.
All of these face the Atlantic, share the North Atlantic Drift and lie in the path of westerly depressions, which is why they have the same climate.

Moving east, away from the Atlantic, winters become colder, summers warmer, the annual range larger and rainfall lower, with a summer maximum (most rain falls in summer). This is the continental influence (the effect of being far from the sea).
The change is gradual, so the boundary of a climatic region is a transition zone, not a line.
notes.tip: Describe the eastward change in words, without numbers. The expected Higher answer includes North West Europe and the eastward transition.

notes.h: Climate and the region's other features
notes.b: Climate shapes more than the weather. In a cool temperate oceanic region it also influences what grows naturally and how the land is farmed.
points: Natural vegetation is deciduous forest (trees that lose their leaves in winter), mainly oak and ash.
Soils are brown earth, the typical soil under deciduous forest.
Grass grows for most of the year, because winters are mild and rain falls in every month. This favours pastoral farming (rearing animals on grass) in Ireland, mainly cattle and dairying.
notes.tip: The Higher answer links climate to vegetation and farming, so finish a climate answer with deciduous forest, brown earth and pastoral farming.

notes.b: Geomorphology is the study of landforms (natural features of the land) and how they formed. A geomorphological region is an area with a distinctive landscape produced by the same rock type, geological structure (how rocks are arranged and folded) or landforming processes.
points: Three settings are studied here: the Burren (a karst region), Munster ridge and valley (South Munster) and the Northern European Plain.
notes.tip: A geomorphological region is one with a unique landscape based on rock type, structure or relief. Short questions ask you to name examples: the Burren, Munster ridge and valley, the Northern European Plain, the Wicklow Mountains and the Leinster batholith.

notes.b: The Burren in north-west Co. Clare is a karst region on Carboniferous limestone, a rock that water slowly dissolves. Formation of its landforms is taught in the notes on Landforms associated with particular rock types; here each landform is only named.
points: The name comes from the Irish Boireann, meaning rocky place.
Limestone pavement (a bare, flat expanse of rock): blocks called clints, separated by fissures (cracks) called grikes.
Turloughs: seasonal lakes in hollows, which fill in winter and drain in summer.
Caves: Aillwee Cave and Doolin Cave, which holds the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long.
Mullaghmore: a hill of folded, terraced limestone, an example of how the rock forms stepped slopes.
Very few surface rivers, because drainage is underground: water sinks through the cracks in the limestone.
Glaciation: granite erratics (boulders carried by ice and dropped far from their source) from Connemara rest on the limestone, showing that ice scraped off the soil and exposed the pavement.
notes.tip: The Burren was glaciated. Don't say its karst survived because ice never reached it, which is a known marking-scheme error. The Cliffs of Moher are sandstone, siltstone and shale, not karst limestone, so don't use them as a karst landform. Don't give the Burren's area, because sources disagree.

notes.h: The Burren: plants, land use and tourism
notes.b: The limestone shapes life on the Burren as well as its landforms: it affects which plants grow, how farmers use the land and why visitors come.
points: Plants from Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean environments grow side by side, for example the spring gentian and mountain avens.
Winterage: cattle graze the upland limestone in winter, because the rock stores heat and the ground is dry.
Poulnabrone, a Neolithic (New Stone Age) portal tomb (dolmen, a stone tomb of upright stones with a large capstone), stands on the limestone pavement.
Burren National Park protects part of the area near Mullaghmore.
The Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark (an area recognised internationally for its geological heritage): tourism is a major activity.
notes.tip: Name the Cliffs of Moher only as part of the Geopark. Don't give the National Park's area, because sources disagree.

notes.b: South Munster is a region of Old Red Sandstone ridges alternating with Carboniferous limestone valleys. Its parallel pattern comes from folding of the rocks and then erosion.
points: Armorican folding (a period of crustal folding) about 300 million years ago, on an east-west trend, produced anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds).
Differential erosion (different rocks wearing away at different rates) left the harder sandstone standing as ridges and wore the softer limestone down into valleys.
Ridges (anticlines of sandstone): Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Caha Mountains.
Valleys (synclines of limestone): the Blackwater valley and the Lee valley.

Trellised drainage (a pattern of rivers following parallel valleys, with short links across them): rivers flow east along the valleys. The River Blackwater then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, and reaches the sea at Youghal. The Lee flows east to Cork Harbour.
Drowned valleys at the coast, flooded by the sea, form rias (long, narrow inlets): Bantry Bay, Dingle Bay and the Kenmare River.
Human consequences: towns, routes and fertile farmland lie in the valleys, while the ridges carry rough grazing, forestry and bog.
notes.tip: Munster ridges are anticlines of sandstone and the valleys are synclines of limestone. Never reverse them.

notes.b: The Northern European Plain is a vast lowland, mostly low, flat or gently rolling, stretching from western France into Russia. Ice and wind shaped its surface, and its flat, fertile land supports many people.
points: Countries crossed: France (north), Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany, Denmark and Poland, and into Russia.
Glacial deposits (material left by ice sheets), including moraines (ridges of rock debris), outwash sands (sand washed out from melting ice) and lakes, shape the north of the plain.
A belt of loess, a wind-blown silt, forms fertile soils along the southern edge.
Loess soils are fertile, so they support crops such as wheat and sugar beet.
The Rhine and Elbe flow north to the North Sea; the Oder and Vistula flow north to the Baltic, which shows the plain slopes gently north.
Polders: land reclaimed from the sea in the Netherlands. The Afsluitdijk, completed in 1932, closed off the Zuiderzee.
Human consequences: fertile farmland, easy movement for transport because the land is flat, dense population and major cities, including Berlin, Warsaw, Hamburg and Amsterdam.
notes.tip: Don't use the Paris Basin as the Northern European Plain example: it is a core region and a sedimentary basin.

notes.b: Each of the three regions is defined by a different criterion, which shows how geomorphology can be used to define regions.
points: The Burren is defined by its rock type, Carboniferous limestone, because that rock produces its karst landforms.
Munster ridge and valley is defined by its geological structure, folded sandstone and limestone, because the folds gave alternating ridges and valleys.
The Northern European Plain is defined by its relief and its surface deposits, glacial and loess, because it is flat and its surface is made of these materials.

The Wicklow Mountains and the Leinster batholith (a huge mass of granite) are granite uplands, also classed as geomorphological regions; their landforms are taught in the notes on Landforms associated with particular rock types.
notes.tip: Exams ask how geomorphology can be used to define regions. Say that rock type, structure and relief are the criteria, one for each example. The Ordinary 30-mark question asks you to describe and explain two region types, and for this subsection the Burren or Munster suits the geomorphological type. Don't call the Mezzogiorno or the West of Ireland physical regions, because they are peripheral (socio-economic) regions.

keyTerms.definition: An area of the earth's surface that shares one or more criteria which make it different from the areas around it.
The characteristics used to identify and define a region, such as climate, language or wealth.
A band of gradual change between two regions, which replaces a sharp boundary for physical and cultural regions.
A large area with similar temperature, precipitation and seasonal pattern, usually with similar vegetation and soils.
The climate of Ireland and North West Europe: mild winters, cool summers, a small temperature range and rain in every month.
A warm ocean current, the extension of the Gulf Stream, which keeps winters mild in north-western Europe.
Rain caused when moist air is forced up over mountains, cools and releases its moisture.
The drier lee side of mountains, sheltered from prevailing winds, as on Ireland's east.
An area with a distinctive landscape produced by the same rock type, geological structure or landforming processes.
A landscape of limestone shaped by solution, with pavements, caves and few surface rivers.
A clint is a block of limestone pavement; a grike is a fissure separating one clint from the next.
A seasonal lake in a hollow of limestone that fills in winter and drains in summer.
The grazing of cattle on upland limestone in winter, when the rock stores heat and the ground is dry.
An anticline is an upfold of rock layers; a syncline is a downfold.
A drowned river valley on the coast, formed when the sea floods the lower end of a valley.
A wind-blown silt deposit that forms fertile soils, here along the southern edge of the Northern European Plain.
Land reclaimed from the sea and protected from flooding by embankments.

factCards.term: Regions at different scales: give one example at each scale
factCards.definition: Local: Co. Clare (or a city's hinterland); national: the West of Ireland; continental: North West Europe; global: the Islamic world.

factCards.term: Climatic regions in matching questions: three types and their examples
factCards.definition: Cool temperate oceanic: Ireland and North West Europe. Warm temperate oceanic: the Mediterranean type, with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. Hot desert: e.g. the Sahara.

factCards.term: Cool temperate oceanic climate: Ireland's temperature figures
factCards.definition: Met Éireann long-term averages: mean January (coldest month) about 4–7°C; mean July (warmest month) about 14–16°C; so the annual range is only about 10°C. Snow is rare on low ground; rain falls in every month.

factCards.term: Annual rainfall across Ireland: the west–east figures
factCards.definition: About 1,000–1,250 mm a year across much of the west and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains, but only about 750 mm in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin, which lies in a rain shadow.

factCards.term: Wet days and sunshine in Ireland: the west–east contrast
factCards.definition: About 150 wet days (days with measurable rain) a year on the east and south-east coasts, rising to about 225 a year in parts of the west. The south-east is the sunniest region.

factCards.term: Why Ireland has a cool temperate oceanic climate: six controls
factCards.definition: Latitude (about 51.5°N to 55.5°N, moderate sun angle); the North Atlantic Drift (mild winters, ice-free coasts); maritime influence (small range); prevailing south-westerlies off the Atlantic; frequent Atlantic depressions; relief rain on western mountains.

factCards.term: North West Europe: which countries share Ireland's climate, and why
factCards.definition: Ireland, Britain, north-west France (Brittany), Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and coastal Norway. All face the Atlantic, share the North Atlantic Drift and lie in the path of westerly depressions.

factCards.term: Cool temperate oceanic region: how the climate changes moving east across Europe
factCards.definition: Away from the Atlantic, winters get colder, summers warmer, the annual range larger and rainfall lower, with a summer maximum (continental influence). The change is gradual, so the region's boundary is a transition zone, not a line.

factCards.term: Cool temperate oceanic region: natural vegetation, soils and farming
factCards.definition: Deciduous forest, mainly oak and ash; brown earth soils; grass grows for most of the year, which favours pastoral farming in Ireland, mainly cattle and dairying.

factCards.term: The Burren: location, rock, name and evidence of glaciation
factCards.definition: North-west Co. Clare, on Carboniferous limestone; the name comes from the Irish Boireann, meaning rocky place. Granite erratics from Connemara rest on the limestone, showing that ice scraped off the soil and exposed the pavement.

factCards.term: The Burren: five karst features, naming the caves and the hill
factCards.definition: Limestone pavement of clints and grikes; turloughs; Aillwee Cave and Doolin Cave, which holds the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long; Mullaghmore, a hill of folded, terraced limestone; very few surface rivers, as drainage is underground.

factCards.term: The Burren: plant life, farming, heritage and protection
factCards.definition: Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants side by side (spring gentian, mountain avens); winterage cattle grazing; Poulnabrone, a Neolithic portal tomb on the pavement; Burren National Park near Mullaghmore; the Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark.

factCards.term: Munster ridge and valley: how the landscape formed
factCards.definition: Armorican folding about 300 million years ago (east–west) made anticlines and synclines; differential erosion left the harder Old Red Sandstone as ridges and wore the Carboniferous limestone into valleys, which hold the towns, routes and best farmland.

factCards.term: Munster ridge and valley: named ridges, valleys and rias
factCards.definition: Sandstone ridges (anticlines): Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee, Knockmealdown and Caha Mountains. Limestone valleys (synclines): the Blackwater and Lee valleys. Rias: Bantry Bay, Dingle Bay and the Kenmare River.

factCards.term: River Blackwater: how its course shows trellised drainage
factCards.definition: It flows east along its limestone valley between parallel sandstone ridges, through Mallow, Fermoy and Lismore, with tributaries flowing off the ridges at right angles; then it turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to reach the sea at Youghal.

factCards.term: Northern European Plain: extent and rivers
factCards.definition: A vast, low, flat to gently rolling lowland from northern France through Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany, Denmark and Poland into Russia. The Rhine and Elbe flow north to the North Sea; the Oder and Vistula flow north to the Baltic.

factCards.term: Northern European Plain: surface deposits and farming
factCards.definition: Glacial deposits (moraines, outwash sands and lakes) shape the north; a belt of fertile loess, a wind-blown silt, along the southern edge grows wheat and sugar beet.

factCards.term: Northern European Plain: polders and human consequences
factCards.definition: Polders are reclaimed from the sea in the Netherlands: the Afsluitdijk, completed 1932, closed off the Zuiderzee. Flat, fertile land gives easy transport, a dense population and major cities such as Berlin, Warsaw, Hamburg and Amsterdam.

factCards.term: Three geomorphological regions: the criterion that defines each
factCards.definition: The Burren: rock type (Carboniferous limestone). Munster ridge and valley: geological structure (folded sandstone and limestone). Northern European Plain: relief and surface deposits (glacial, loess).

questions.prompt: Using a climatic region you have studied, explain how climate can be used to identify a region.
questions.model: Definition: a climatic region is a large area with similar temperature, precipitation and seasonal pattern, usually with similar vegetation and soils. Take the cool temperate oceanic climate of Ireland. Give the temperature figures (mild winters, cool summers, a small annual range) and the rainfall figures, with rain in every month and no dry season. Explain the controls: latitude, the North Atlantic Drift, the maritime influence, prevailing south-westerly winds, Atlantic depressions and their fronts, and relief rainfall. Describe the variation within Ireland: the wetter west, the rain shadow in the east, the sunnier south-east and the milder coasts. Show how the climate extends across North West Europe and changes eastward into a continental climate with colder winters, warmer summers, a larger range, lower rainfall and a summer maximum, so the boundary is a transition zone. Finish with the links to vegetation (deciduous oak and ash forest, brown earth) and farming (grass for most of the year, supporting cattle and dairying). Do not include geomorphology.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain two geomorphological regions you have studied.
questions.model: Choose the Burren (karst) and Munster ridge and valley. For the Burren: Carboniferous limestone; name the landforms (limestone pavement of clints and grikes, turloughs, caves) and explain that drainage is underground with few surface rivers; explain that glaciation exposed the pavement; describe the plants, winterage grazing, Poulnabrone and the UNESCO Geopark with its tourism. For Munster ridge and valley: east-west folding about 300 million years ago; Old Red Sandstone ridges and Carboniferous limestone valleys, named; the trellised drainage of the Blackwater and the Lee; rias at the coast; human consequences of towns, routes and farmland in the valleys and rough grazing, forestry and bog on the ridges. Give no more formation detail than one bullet per landform.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a region, and give one example of a region at a local scale and one at a continental scale.
questions.model: A region is an area of the earth's surface that shares one or more criteria which make it different from the areas around it. Local scale: Co. Clare (or the Burren). Continental scale: North West Europe.
